# The Question

Is there some sort of seasonality in the types of crimes over 10 years in Berkeley? Does the mix of crime types shift with the seasons?

# Loading the data

The dataset I will use is the Berkeley Police Department’s Cases from 2016 to current, in which each row is a police-reported case, and the columns are that case’s ID number, the time and date at which it occurred, the incident type, statute, statute description, block address, city, and ZIP code.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import periodogram, welch
```

```{python}
bpd = pd.read_csv("data/bpd-2016-now.csv")
bpd.head()
```

# Cleaning the Data

After printing the first rows of data, I can see that I am interested mostly in the `Case_Number`, `Occurred_Datetime`, and `Incident_Type` columns. These columns are the only ones that are relevant for my analysis.

```{python}
bpd = bpd[["Case_Number", "Occurred_Datetime", "Incident_Type"]]
bpd.head()
```

```{python}
# parse date time column
bpd["Occurred_Datetime"] = pd.to_datetime(bpd["Occurred_Datetime"])
bpd["Month"] = bpd["Occurred_Datetime"].dt.month
bpd["Year"] = bpd["Occurred_Datetime"].dt.year

# add season column
def get_season(month):
    if month in [12, 1, 2]:
        return "Winter"
    elif month in [3, 4, 5]:
        return "Spring"
    elif month in [6, 7, 8]:
        return "Summer"
    else:
        return "Fall"

bpd["Season"] = bpd["Month"].apply(get_season)
bpd.head()
```

In `Incident_Type`, there are the following 40 entries:

```{python}
print(bpd["Incident_Type"].unique())
print(bpd["Incident_Type"].nunique())
```

The primary ones I originally wanted to focus on in terms of identifying seasonality are: Robbery, Assault/Battery Felony, Vehicle Stolen, Burglary Residential, Homicide, Driving under the influence, Alcohol Related Offense, Child Abuse, and Gun/Weapon. I believed these would be the most revealing in terms of seasonality.

However, after looking at my data, I can see a lot of those categories don't have a lot of observations, so instead I will focus on the categories with the most data. Those are:

```{python}
# Prep to aggregate to weekly counts per crime type
bpd["Week"] = bpd["Occurred_Datetime"].dt.to_period("W")
bpd.head()

# focus on the major categories
major_crimes = ["Theft Misdemeanor (Under $950)", "Burglary Auto", "Vehicle Stolen", "Disturbance", "Theft Felony (over $950)", "Vandalism", "Burglary Residential", "Assault/Battery Misdemeanor"]

```

```{python}
# Remove duplicates introduced by dropping the specific Statute_Description column
bpd_clean = bpd.drop_duplicates(subset="Case_Number")
bpd_clean.head()

counts = bpd_clean["Incident_Type"].value_counts()
print(counts.to_string())

# Filtering to rows matching major categories
bpd_filtered = bpd_clean[bpd_clean["Incident_Type"].isin(major_crimes)]
bpd.head()
```



Next I will continue preparing the data to week.

```{python}
# Weekly counts per crime type
weekly = (
    bpd_filtered
    .groupby(["Week", "Incident_Type"])
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="Count")
    .pivot(index="Week", columns="Incident_Type", values="Count")
    .fillna(0)
    .sort_index()
)

weekly.head()
```

## Data Visualization

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(16, 20))
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, crime in enumerate(major_crimes):
    # aggregate to monthly counts
    monthly = (
        bpd_filtered[bpd_filtered["Incident_Type"] == crime]
        .groupby(["Year", "Month"])
        .size()
        .reset_index(name="Count")

plt.suptitle("Monthly Crime Counts by Type (2016 to Present)", fontsize=16, fontweight="bold", y=1.01)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Power Spectral Analysis

I will conduct Power Spectral Density using Welch's method. Welch smooths the raw periodigram by averaging the overlapping segments, which reduces noise so peaks are easier to interpret when they occur.

```{python power spectral analysis}
fs = 1  # 1 sample per week
freq_labels = {1/52: "Annual", 1/26: "Semi-annual", 1/13: "Quarterly", 1/4: "Monthly"}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(weekly.columns), 1, figsize=(10, 3 * len(weekly.columns)), sharex=True)

for ax, crime in zip(axes, weekly.columns):
    signal = weekly[crime].values
    freqs, psd = welch(signal, fs=fs, nperseg=52)  # nperseg=52 = 1yr window

    ax.semilogy(freqs, psd, color="steelblue", linewidth=1.5)
    ax.set_title(crime, fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_ylabel("Power")

    # Marking known seasonal frequencies
    for freq, label in freq_labels.items():
        ax.axvline(x=freq, color="red", linestyle="--", alpha=0.5, linewidth=1)
        ax.text(freq, ax.get_ylim()[1], label, rotation=90, fontsize=7,
                color="red", va="top", ha="right")


axes[-1].set_xlabel("Frequency (cycles per week)")
fig.suptitle("Welch Power Spectral Density by Crime Type", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", y=1.01)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The results of these power spectral analysis charts are quite clear in terms of identifying where there exists periodicity in the various crime categories:

- Theft Misdemeanor (Under $950)

- Burglary Auto

- Vehicle Stolen

- Disturbance

- Theft Felony (over $950)

- Vandalism

- Burglary Residential

- Assault/Battery Misdemeanor


# Short-time Fourier Transform

Next, I will identify if the seasonal structure has shifted over the decade. This could be especially interesting after 2020.

```{python}
from scipy.signal import stft
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors

ncols = 3
nrows = math.ceil(len(major_crimes) / ncols)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(18, 4 * nrows))
axes = axes.flatten()

# Get the start year for x-axis labels
start_year = weekly.index[0].start_time.year

for i, crime in enumerate(major_crimes):
    signal = weekly[crime].values
    
    # STFT: nperseg=52 = 1-year window, noverlap=26 = 50% overlap
    freqs, times, Zxx = stft(signal, fs=1, nperseg=52, noverlap=26)
    
    # Plot only frequencies up to semi-annual (1/26) for readability
    freq_mask = freqs <= 1/13
    
    im = axes[i].pcolormesh(
        times, freqs[freq_mask], np.abs(Zxx[freq_mask]),
        shading="gouraud", cmap="inferno"
    )
    
    # Mark annual and semi-annual lines
    for freq, label in [(1/52, "Annual"), (1/26, "Semi-annual")]:
        axes[i].axhline(y=freq, color="cyan", linestyle="--", linewidth=1, alpha=0.7)
        axes[i].text(times[-1], freq, label, fontsize=7, color="cyan", va="bottom", ha="right")
    
    # X-axis: convert week indices to years
    n_weeks = len(signal)
    tick_positions = np.linspace(0, n_weeks, 6)
    tick_labels = [str(int(start_year + t / 52)) for t in tick_positions]
    axes[i].set_xticks(tick_positions)
    axes[i].set_xticklabels(tick_labels, fontsize=8)
    
    axes[i].set_title(crime, fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
    axes[i].set_ylabel("Frequency", fontsize=8)
    axes[i].set_xlabel("Year", fontsize=8)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes[i], label="|STFT|")

# Hide unused plot
for j in range(i + 1, len(axes)):
    axes[j].set_visible(False)

fig.suptitle("Short-Time Fourier Transform by Crime Type", 
             fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

These plots indicate that Berkeley has become safer with time, which is a surprising result. Below are the trends by category:

Strong annual periodicity:

- Burglary Residential: bright, consistent band right at the annual line, persisting until 2023.

- Vehicle Stolen: clear annual signal, especially 2019-2025, which brightens after the pandemic.

- Theft Misdemeanor: bright annual signal, consistent throughout.

Strong semi-annual periodicity:

- Burglary Auto: has some flares that are bright in the semi-annual band, but mostly bright in the annual area. Very bright 2016-2019, with a marked decrease during COVID years, and a smaller resurgence in 2021-2023. 

- Theft Felony: shows some annual periodicity but its not as consistent of a horizontal band like for Theft Misdimeanor. Much brighter after the pandemic years. 

Mixed/diffuse signals:

- Disturbance: energy is spread across low frequencies rather than concentrated at annual or semi-annual, suggesting slow trends rather than sharp seasonal cycles.

- Vandalism: similar to disturbance, diffused low-frequency energy. Some trends annually. 

- Assault/Battery Misdemeanor: relatively dim overall but some annual structure visible.

# Time Lagged Regression

Building weekly counts per crime type:

```{python}
# Convert Period index to timestamp for TLR compatibility
weekly_tlr = weekly.copy()
```

For every crime type, creating the lagged variables and running the regression:

### Residential Burglaries

```{python}
import statsmodels.api as sm

crime = 'Burglary Residential'

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['y'] = weekly_tlr[crime]
df['lag52'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(52)
df['lag51'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(51)
df['lag53'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(53)
df = df.dropna()

X = sm.add_constant(df[['lag52', 'lag51', 'lag53']])
y = df['y']

model = sm.NegativeBinomial(y, X).fit()
print(model.summary())
```

Results: lag52 and lag51 are both statistically significant, meaning knowing how many residential burglaries happened exactly one year ago meaningfully predicts this week's count. 

LLR p = 0.0006 so the model as a whole is significant. 

Alpha = 0.0803 so overdispersion is quite low, residential burglary counts are relatively well-behaved and consistent week to week compared to rarer crimes

### Vehicle Stolen

```{python}
crime = 'Vehicle Stolen'

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['y'] = weekly_tlr[crime]
df['lag52'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(52)
df['lag51'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(51)
df['lag53'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(53)
df = df.dropna()

X = sm.add_constant(df[['lag52', 'lag51', 'lag53']])
y = df['y']

model = sm.NegativeBinomial(y, X).fit()
print(model.summary())
```

Results: lag51 is significant, but lag52 and lag53 are not. Indicates that seasonality exists but doesn't repeat on a precise week-for-week basis. 

LLR p = 5.1e-08 indicates that the model is highly significant.

For vehicle theft specifically, this makes sense: the seasonal peak is likely to shift with weather and opportunity rather than falling on a specific calendar week each year.

### Theft Misdimeanor

```{python}
crime = 'Theft Misdemeanor (Under $950)'

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['y'] = weekly_tlr[crime]
df['lag52'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(52)
df['lag51'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(51)
df['lag53'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(53)
df = df.dropna()

X = sm.add_constant(df[['lag52', 'lag51', 'lag53']])
y = df['y']

model = sm.NegativeBinomial(y, X).fit()
print(model.summary())
```

Results: lag52 and lag51 are not siginifcant, but lag53 is. This could mean that the seasonal pattern takes just over a year to repeat, or the peak drifts later in the calendar each year. 

LLR p = 0.0008 so likely the model is significant despite the fact that individual lag pattern is asymmetric.

Alpha = 0.0182 so overdispersion is low and weekly counts are relatively stable

### Burglary Auto

```{python}
crime = 'Burglary Auto'

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['y'] = weekly_tlr[crime]
df['lag52'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(52)
df['lag51'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(51)
df['lag53'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(53)
df = df.dropna()

X = sm.add_constant(df[['lag52', 'lag51', 'lag53']])
y = df['y']

model = sm.NegativeBinomial(y, X).fit()
print(model.summary())
```

Results: no signficant p values and the LLR p-value indicates the model is not significant. This makes sense because, in the STFT, burglary auto was shown to have more semi-annual trends, and not as much annual trends. 

I will do another regression at lag26 to possibly identify semi-annual trends:

```{python}
crime = 'Burglary Auto'

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['y'] = weekly_tlr[crime]
df['lag26'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(26)
df['lag25'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(25)
df['lag27'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(27)
df = df.dropna()

X = sm.add_constant(df[['lag26', 'lag25', 'lag27']])
y = df['y']

model = sm.NegativeBinomial(y, X).fit()
print(model.summary())
```

After this, I can see that each lag around the six-month mark is significant, and the coefficients are all similar (0.0056, 0.0073, 0.0063). Auto burglary likely has a semi-annual trend structure.

Also computing for semi-annual:

```{python}
crime = 'Theft Felony (over $950)'

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['y'] = weekly_tlr[crime]
df['lag26'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(26)
df['lag25'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(25)
df['lag27'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(27)
df = df.dropna()

X = sm.add_constant(df[['lag26', 'lag25', 'lag27']])
y = df['y']

model = sm.NegativeBinomial(y, X).fit()
print(model.summary())
```

Results: it seems clear that the annual lag52 is weak and inconclusive (lag52 p = 0.096, lag51 p = 0.791, lag53 p = 0.072) although the model is significant (LLR p = 0.0019). However, at the semi-annual level, two p values are significant (lag26 p = 0.001, lag25 p = 0.022, lag27 p = 0.107). Its dominant seasonal structure is semi-annual, not annual.

```{python}
crime = 'Assault/Battery Misdemeanor'

df = pd.DataFrame()
```

```{python}
df['lag26'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(26)
df['lag25'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(25)
df['lag27'] = weekly_tlr[crime].shift(27)
```

Results: in this case, for annual lags, lag51 and lag53 are significant, but lag52 is not (lag52 p = 0.081, lag51 p = 0.015, lag53 p = 0.000). 

For semi-annual lags, all lags are significant (lag26 p = 0.036, lag25 p = 0.001, lag27 p = 0.000). 

Assault/Battery Misdemeanor is the only crime type in this 
analysis to show evidence of both annual and semi-annual periodicity, 
suggesting a seasonal structure that works at different time scales at the same time.


# Plotting Counts

By months:

```{python}
# Average count by month across all years
monthly_avg = (
    bpd_filtered
    .groupby(["Incident_Type", "Month"])
    .size()
    .reset_index(name="Count")
    .groupby(["Incident_Type", "Month"])["Count"]
    .mean()
    .reset_index()
)

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(16, 20))
axes = axes.flatten()
month_names = ['Jan','Feb','Mar','Apr','May','Jun','Jul','Aug','Sep','Oct','Nov','Dec']

for i, crime in enumerate(major_crimes):
    data = monthly_avg[monthly_avg["Incident_Type"] == crime]
    axes[i].bar(data["Month"], data["Count"], color="steelblue", alpha=0.7)
    axes[i].set_xticks(range(1, 13))
    axes[i].set_xticklabels(month_names, rotation=45)
    axes[i].set_title(crime, fontsize=11, fontweight="bold")
    axes[i].set_ylabel("Avg Monthly Count")

plt.suptitle("Average Monthly Crime Count by Type", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

By season:

```{python}
season_order = ["Winter", "Spring", "Summer", "Fall"]
colors = {"Winter": "steelblue", "Spring": "mediumseagreen", "Summer": "tomato", "Fall": "darkorange"}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(16, 20))
axes = axes.flatten()

for i, crime in enumerate(major_crimes):
    seasonal = (
        bpd_filtered[bpd_filtered["Incident_Type"] == crime]
        .groupby("Season")
        .size()
        .reindex(season_order)  # ensures consistent order
        .reset_index(name="Count")
    )
    
    bar_colors = [colors[s] for s in season_order]
    axes[i].bar(season_order, seasonal["Count"], color=bar_colors, alpha=0.8)
    axes[i].set_title(crime, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    axes[i].set_xlabel("Season")
    axes[i].set_ylabel("Total Count")

plt.suptitle("Total Crime Count by Season", fontsize=16, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
